message.content:
**Decision: do not deploy as proposed, and do not certify tenant isolation.**

Node's docs say the Permission Model "does not protect against malicious code," is a "seat belt" for trusted code, and is "**not**... a security boundary against intentional misuse or a compromised process" (https://nodejs.org/download/release/v24.21.0/docs/api/permissions.html#permission-model; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nodejs/node/v24.21.0/SECURITY.md#permission-model-boundaries-permission). The policy trusts the code it runs, which "inherits all the privileges of the execution user," and treats untrusted users' code as an application-level issue (SECURITY.md#the-nodejs-threat-model). Customer uploads are untrusted, so the only tenant boundary can be OS-level (separate users, seccomp/AppArmor, VMs) — the docs' own recommendation (permissions.html#process_debugprocess-and-cross-process-inspector-activation).

**Assumptions requiring change**
- `/srv/jobs/*.js`: after `*` all characters are ignored, so it behaves as `/srv/jobs/*` — read access to the entire tree, including other tenants' uploads (permissions.html#file-system-permissions). Grant exact per-job files instead.
- Relative symlinks: "Symbolic links will be followed even to locations outside of the set of paths that access has been granted to. Relative symbolic links may allow access to arbitrary files and directories." Granted paths must contain none (permissions.html#limitations-and-known-issues); resolve realpaths before launch.
- Pre-opened fd: "Using existing file descriptors via the node:fs module bypasses the Permission Model," and `drop()` does not revoke open descriptors (permissions.html#permission-model-constraints). Treat the fd as fully privileged; never hand it to amalgamated tenants.
- `--env-file`: read before the model initializes, therefore "not subject to the rules of the Permission Model," and it applies Node-configuring variables such as `NODE_OPTIONS` (cli.html#--env-filefile). Whether that unlocks further privileges is UNVERIFIED.
- Workers: version-matched sources conflict. permissions.html says "The model does not inherit to a worker thread"; SECURITY.md says workers "inherit the permission restrictions of their parent process." Do not rely on assumed inheritance; resolve via release tests/issues.
- Ungated: `node:sqlite` file access; `process._debugProcess()` (SIGUSR1) (same permission sections).
- Staging: `--permission-audit` needs no `--allow-*` flags; if both flags are passed, enforce mode wins (cli.html#--permission-audit).

**Fit use:** blast-radius reduction and audit-mode grant discovery for trusted application code — never sole isolation for hostile code.

Also note: --permission-audit "does not require --permission", and --allow-* flags are not needed in audit mode. So staging with --permission-audit plus allow flags is fine but the allow flags are partly moot. Also if both --permission and --permission-audit are given, enforce wins.

Wildcard: --allow-fs-read=/srv/jobs/*.js behaves like /srv/jobs/* — grants read to all matching prefix, e.g. /srv/jobs/other.js and /srv/jobs/anything. Actually the doc says "After passing a wildcard character (*) all subsequent characters will be ignored. For example: /home/*.js will work similar to /home/*." So the pattern /srv/jobs/*.js → /srv/jobs/* — grants read to the entire /srv/jobs/ directory tree. That's material: one tenant's job can read all other tenants' scripts.

Also directory existence: if /srv/jobs exists, --allow-fs-read=/srv/jobs would be auto-expanded to /srv/jobs/*. And "If you want to allow access to a folder that does not exist yet, make sure to explicitly include the wildcard".

Symlinks: documented limitation — symlinks followed even outside granted paths; relative symlinks may allow access to arbitrary files and directories; must ensure no granted paths contain relative symlinks. Since job directories "may contain relative symbolic links", this is a concrete documented break.

Existing fd: "Using existing file descriptors via the node:fs module bypasses the Permission Model." So the pre-opened fd is outside the permission model. Also permission.drop() doesn't revoke open fds.

--env-file: reads before permission model init, not subject to permission rules. Note: --env-file applies env vars, including NODE_OPTIONS — that's a real escalation vector worth mentioning? Documented: "The environment variables which configure Node.js, such as NODE_OPTIONS, are parsed and applied." Hmm — that's about the env file content shaping Node config; combined with the fact the file is not permission-checked. I can mention: the env file is read pre-permission-model and its content can set Node-configured env vars like NODE_OPTIONS (documented). That's a documented footgun but the operator passing --env-file is an operator-controlled flag; SECURITY.md says operator-controlled flags are the operator's responsibility. I should mark the escalation implication carefully — the doc says env vars that configure Node.js such as NODE_OPTIONS are parsed and applied. Whether that can unlock flags beyond the model's scope is not established by the fetched text → mark as UNVERIFIED.

Node's security policy: permission model is "designed to reduce blast radius of mistakes in trusted application code, not to act as a security boundary against intentional misuse or a compromised process"; "Node.js trusts the code it is asked to run, including JavaScript... The code run inherits all the privileges of the execution user"; and "Permitting untrusted users to define custom code that executes with the application's privileges" is not a Node vulnerability.

Also: doesn't restrict network; doesn't restrict node:sqlite; process._debugProcess cross-process inspector (SIGUSR1) reachable with no grants; also could mention the need for OS isolation.

Also the read grant covers only fs module: "It does not guarantee that users will not be able to access the file system through other means, such as through the node:sqlite module."

Answer question: "Do these documents let you certify this deployment's tenant isolation?" No.

Recommendations (mine, marked as recommendations): don't use --permission alone as sole boundary; add OS-level isolation (separate OS users, seccomp/AppArmor, containers) per docs' own suggestion; avoid relative symlinks in granted paths, resolve realpath and validate before running; treat the inherited fd as fully privileged to whatever it points at, pass only pre-validated narrow fds (or avoid); keep env file outside job-controlled paths and don't let it carry Node-configuring variables; use --permission in staging to record exact grants but note audit mode doesn't need allow flags; wildcard argument should be a single explicit file grant per job, e.g. --allow-fs-read=/srv/jobs/<jobid>/job.js (note still wildcard/prefix behavior on the last component, so use a non-ambiguous per-job dir) — careful: the doc says wildcard expansion applies with the prefix before '*'; a path without '*' is a literal exact file. Yes: "--allow-fs-read=/tmp/ --allow-fs-read=/HOME/.gitignore". So exact file paths are fine.

Also: entrypoints are implicitly readable — so the job's own entry script is implicitly readable; explicit grant arguably unneeded. But if the loaded script is the entrypoint, it's auto-allowed; the explicit wildcard grant is the problem.
